title: A Norwegian Pop Star Embraces a Medieval Mystic
author: Matthew Schmitz
content:
![A Norwegian Pop Star Embraces a Medieval
Mystic](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/IMG_5388-1.jpg)

Norway is one of the world's [_least
religious_](https://ess.sikt.no/en/datafile/98b539ee-63f4-4803-a384-a8d05293894c?tab=1&elems=dc6df418-c51f-405e-989b-a6f12c60f214&ref=compactmag.com)
countries, but the spirit is moving some of its most interesting artists. Jon
Fosse, the Nobel-winning novelist, is a Catholic who writes of lonely men's
encounters with divine providence. Karl Ove Knausgaard, a writer known for
minute realism, has [_turned to_](https://thepointmag.com/criticism/after-the-
end/?ref=compactmag.com) supernatural themes. And now Susanne Sundfør, an
independent musician known for snappy dance numbers and tales of heartbreak,
has released _Revelations of Divine Love_ , a record whose lyrics are drawn
entirely from the writings of the fourteenth-century mystic Julian of Norwich.

Some religious artworks are the expressions of broadly believing cultures--
think Bach's _Mass in B Minor_ or the cathedral at Chartres. But today,
religious art often has a different character. Rather than giving voice to the
dominant outlook, religion becomes a site of resistance to mainstream values.
In this way, it can prove attractive to people who normally would not be drawn
to dogmatic belief.

> "Religion becomes a site of resistance to mainstream values."

"There is a mysticism wave happening among artists in Europe," Sundfør tells
me. Her new album, co-written with the organist Kit Downes, exemplifies this
trend. Though Sundfør is not Catholic or avowedly Christian, she has produced
a remarkable piece of sacred music, her supple voice lending poignancy to the
unexpected affirmation that God is what "[_Holy Church preacheth and teacheth
thee_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DAfDiM9BbOw&ref=compactmag.com)."

Sundfør came across Julian's writings at a time when a friend of hers was
suffering from breast cancer--and joining the Catholic Church. What she found
surprised her. "It felt like something a guru in the '60s New Age movement
would write, but it was Christian. And I hadn't really been introduced to that
kind of Christianity before."

Part of the attraction was feminist, though not in the conventional sense of
that word. In Julian's writing, and in Catholic piety generally, Sundfør finds
compelling images of womanhood. "The religious story that makes the most sense
to me is Jesus and Mary," she says. "I think it's what a society should be
based on, mother and child."

This vision of womanhood is especially attractive in a society that is at once
prurient and censorious. "Sex is very distorted," Sundfør says. "It's either
Puritan or porn." She views sex in religious terms as something positive. "To
me, sex is sacred. I think that's a problem we have around sexuality today,
that it's become sort of secularized, for lack of a better word."

Sundfør's high view of sex and motherhood explains the album's cover art. It
shows a woman giving birth, her face lit with ecstasy. Based on a photo from
the natural birth advocate Ina May Gaskin, it depicts a phenomenon reported by
midwives, in which the woman climaxes during delivery.

Unsurprisingly, the cover art has been censored by music platforms such as
Apple and Spotify. Sundfør hesitated before using it, but she finally decided
that it was necessary to convey her meaning. For her, the image has a specific
theological resonance. "In the Scripture, they say that Mary gave birth
without pain," she notes. "There's a theory within Christianity that Jesus
reversed Adam's sins, Mary reversed Eve's sins"--a reference to the patristic
idea of Mary as the "new Eve." This reversal entailed the lifting of a curse
described in Genesis. "What was the consequence of Eve's misdoings or errors?
She had to have pain in childbirth. And then Mary didn't."

In this way, an explicit image drawn from an alternative birth manual comes to
express a spiritual longing for the restoration of motherhood--so that it
ceases to be painful or despised, and becomes instead an unmixed blessing.

Sundfør's own experience of childbirth helped her understand the words of
Julian. The mystic's [_great theme_](https://firstthings.com/doctor-of-
providence/?ref=compactmag.com) is trust in divine providence--God's control
over all that happens. Thus her famous words, "All shall be well." As Sundfør
notes, midwives often tell mothers to "[_trust the
process_](https://wearedti.com/blogs/news/we-trust-normal-birth-and-parents-
instincts?ref=compactmag.com)" in order to avoid anxiety -- a kind of lesson
in relying on providence.

That trust can be seen on her album's cover and in Julian's writing. "Here is
a woman who is in complete trust of the wonder that is about to happen,"
Sundfør says. "And only then can you sort of give birth to someone in such
ecstasy. So it's like the ultimate image of love, really."

Sundfør understands her exploration of faith as a response to a universal
longing. "I think we're supposed to be religious. I don't think it's natural
for human beings to not be religious," she says. "It creates a vacuum in us,
and we need to fill it with something."

If Sundfør is right, people in secular societies will continue to search for
some source of spiritual meaning. Where will they find it? Ever since she was
a child, Sundfør says, she has been "searching for something bigger." She has
found intimations of that something in the words of a medieval mystic and in
the relationship between Jesus and Mary. "Love really is bigger," she tells
me.
